 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026

M/S PARTHIVI CONSTRUCTION PVT. LTD. & ORS.       APPELLANTS(S)
                               VERSUS
SHRI BHUNESHWAR PRASAD VERMA & ANR.              RESPONDENT(S)
       O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Under the impugned judgment
of the High Court, appellants’ statutory
appeal  under  Section  58  of  the
Chhattisgarh Real Estate (Regulation and
Development) Act, 2016 (for short, the
“Act, 2016”) has been rejected.  The said
appeal had questioned the legality and
propriety of the order dated 26.09.2025
passed by the Chhattisgarh Real Estate
Appellate Tribunal, Raipur (for short,
the “Appellate Tribunal”), whereby the
appeal preferred by the appellants was
dismissed for non-compliance of its order

--- Page 39 ---
2
dated 20.08.2025.
3. On  a  complaint  filed  by
respondent No.1, the Chhattisgarh Real
Estate  Regulatory  Authority  (RERA),
Raipur, passed an order on 27.06.2025
allowing  his  claim  and  directing  the
appellants  to  pay  a  total  sum  of
1,06,79,900/-  to  respondent  No.1-₹
claimant.  Challenging  the  said  order,
appellants preferred an appeal before the
Appellate Tribunal under Section 44 of
the Act, 2016 along with an application
seeking exemption from depositing 30% of
the  amount  awarded  against  respondent
No.1.  The  Tribunal  rejected  the
application and directed the appellants
to deposit the entire amount as awarded
by the RERA.  It is this order of the
Appellate  Tribunal  which  was
unsuccessfully assailed before the High
Court. 
4. Mr.  Sameer  Shrivastava,
learned counsel for the appellants would
submit that even in this Court’s judgment

--- Page 40 ---
3
in  Newtech  Promoters  and  Developers
Private Limited v. State of Uttar Pradesh
& Ors., (2021) 18 SCC 1, there is no such
mandate directing the promoter to deposit
the entire amount of compensation as a
pre-condition  for  hearing  the  appeal.
According to him, the discretion still
lies with the Appellate Authority either
to direct the deposit of 30% of the
awarded amount or such higher percentage
or the total amount.  In this case, the
Appellate Tribunal has not exercised the
discretion and has straightaway directed
the appellants to deposit 100% of the
awarded amount.  Therefore, there being a
failure  to  exercise  the  discretionary
power,  the  High  Court  ought  to  have
interfered with the order passed by the
Appellate Tribunal.
5. Per  contra ,  Mr.  Amrendra
Kumar  Mehta,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondents, would submit that in view of
the judgment passed by this Court in
Newtech Promoters and Developers Private

--- Page 41 ---
4
Limited  (supra), when the award is for
payment of compensation to the consumer,
the entire amount has to be deposited as
a pre-condition for the hearing of the
appeal by the Appellate Tribunal.
6. Having heard learned counsel
for the parties, we are of the considered
view that the point raised in this appeal
is no longer res integra, inasmuch as the
provisions contained in the proviso to
sub-section (5) of Section 43 of the Act,
2016, have already been interpreted by
this Court, holding that where the appeal
is against an order directing payment of
compensation, the promoter is under an
obligation to deposit with the Appellate
Tribunal the total amount to be paid to
the allottee, which includes interest and
compensation imposed upon him.
7.  We may profitably refer to
the observations made by this Court in
Paragraphs 121, 122, 128, 136 and 137 of
the judgment in  Newtech Promoters and
Developers Private Limited (supra):

--- Page 42 ---
5
“121. It may straightaway be noticed that
Section 43(5) of the Act envisages the
filing of an appeal before the Appellate
Tribunal  against  the  order  of  an
Authority or the adjudicating officer by
any  person  aggrieved  and  where  the
promoter intends to appeal against an
order  of  Authority  or  adjudicating
officer against imposition of penalty,
the promoter has to deposit at least 30%
of the penalty amount or such higher
amount  as  may  be  directed  by  the
Appellate Tribunal. Where the appeal is
against any other order which involves
the return of the amount to the allottee,
the  promoter  is  under  obligation  to
deposit with the Appellate Tribunal the
total amount to be paid to the allottee
which includes interest and compensation
imposed on him, if any, or with both, as
the case may be, before the appeal is to
be instituted.
122. The plea advanced by the learned
counsel  for  the  appellants  is  that
substantive right of appeal against an
order of Authority/adjudicating officer
cannot remain dependent on fulfilment of
pre-deposit which is otherwise onerous on
the  builders  alone  and  only  the
builders/promoters who are in appeal are
required to make the pre-deposit to get
the appeal entertained by the Appellate
Tribunal is discriminatory amongst the
stakeholders  as  defined  under  the
provisions of the Act.
xxx xxx xxx
128. There are multiple statutes which
provide a condition of pre-deposit of a

--- Page 43 ---
6
stipulated  statutory  amount  to  be
deposited before an appeal is entertained
by  an  appellate  forum/tribunal  for
reappraisal  of  facts  and  law  at  the
appellate stage and it has been examined
by this Court as well. The proviso to
Section 18 of the  SARFAESI Act, 2002 of
the Act which provides pre-deposit is as
follows:
“18.  Appeal  to  Appellate  Tribunal .—
(1)       *              *              *
Provided further that no appeal shall
be entertained unless the borrower has
deposited  with  the  Appellate  Tribunal
fifty per cent of the amount of debt due
from  him,  as  claimed  by  the  secured
creditors  or  determined  by  the  Debts
Recovery Tribunal, whichever is less:
Provided  also  that  the  Appellate
Tribunal  may,  for  the  reasons  to  be
recorded in writing, reduce the amount to
not less than twenty-five per cent of
debt referred to in the second proviso.”
xxx xxx xxx
136.  In  our  considered  view,  the
obligation cast upon the promoter of pre-
deposit under Section 43(5) of the Act,
being  a  class  in  itself,  and  the
promoters who are in receipt of money
which  is  being  claimed  by  the
homebuyers/allottees  for  refund  and
determined in the first place by the
competent authority, if legislature in
its wisdom intended to ensure that money
once determined by the Authority be saved
if appeal is to be preferred at the

--- Page 44 ---
7
instance  of  the  promoter  after  due
compliance of pre-deposit as envisaged
under Section 43(5) of the Act, in no
circumstance can be said to be onerous as
prayed for or in violation of Article 14
or Article 19(1)( g) of the Constitution
of India.
137. To examine this question, it will be
apposite to take note of Section 40 that
states regarding the recovery of interest
or  penalty  or  compensation  to  be
recovered as arrears of land revenue, and
reads as under:
“40. Recovery of interest or penalty or
compensation and enforcement of order,
etc.—
(1) If a promoter or an allottee or a
real estate agent, as the case may be,
fails to pay any interest or penalty or
compensation  imposed  on  him,  by  the
adjudicating officer or the Regulatory
Authority or the Appellate Authority, as
the case may be, under this Act or the
rules and regulations made thereunder, it
shall be recoverable from such promoter
or allottee or real estate agent, in such
manner as may be prescribed as an arrears
of land revenue.
(2) If any adjudicating officer or the
Regulatory  Authority  or  the  Appellate
Tribunal, as the case may be, issues any
order or directs any person to do any
act, or refrain from doing any act, which
it is empowered to do under this Act or
the rules or regulations made thereunder,
then in case of failure by any person to
comply with such order or direction, the

--- Page 45 ---
8
same shall be enforced, in such manner as
may be prescribed.”
8. It is also to be seen that
the Act, 2016, has been enacted with the
objects and reasons mentioned therein,
which  include  ensuring  greater
accountability  towards  consumers,  to
significantly reduce frauds and delays,
and also the current high transaction
costs, and to balance the interests of
consumers  and  promoters  by  imposing
certain responsibilities on both, and to
bring  transparency  to  the  contractual
conditions,  set  minimum  standards  of
accountability and a fast-track dispute
resolution mechanism. It is also enacted
to impose liability upon the promoter to
pay such compensation to the allottees,
in  the  manner  as  provided  under  the
proposed  legislation,  in  case  the
promoter  fails  to  discharge  any
obligation  imposed  on  him  under  the
proposed  legislation.  Thus,  the  basic
object for the enactment of the Act,
2016, is the protection of the interests

--- Page 46 ---
9
of the consumers and to ensure greater
accountability  and  liability  upon  the
promoter. Therefore, in order to achieve
the object for which the Act has been
enacted, the proviso to sub-section (5)
of  Section  43  has  provided  for  the
deposit  of  the  total  amount  of
compensation  and  interest  awarded,  in
case the promoter desires to go in appeal
challenging  the  Award  of  such
compensation.
10. In view of the above, we
are  of  the  considered  view  that  the
Appellate Tribunal was fully justified in
rejecting  appellants’  request  for
exempting from deposit of 30% of the
awarded amount, for the simple reason
that under the law as interpreted by this
Court in Newtech Promoters and Developers
Private Limited  (supra), the appellants
are under an obligation to deposit the
entire amount of compensation.

--- Page 47 ---
10
11. The  appeal  fails  and  is,
accordingly, dismissed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NOS. 206-210 OF 2003
N. RAVI & ORS. PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
SPEAKER, LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY,
CHENNAI & ORS.
RESPONDENT(S)
W I T H
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 508 OF 2003
O R D E R
1. The genesis of the present writ petitions lies in a series of
articles published in the daily newspaper The Hindu on 12.04.2003,
13.04.2003, 23.04.2003 and 25.04.2003, reporting on the proceedings
of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. Thereafter, on 26.04.2003,
The Murasoli carried a verbatim Tamil translation of the editorial
published in  The Hindu  on 25.04.2003. On the basis of these
publications, the Speaker referred the matter to the Committee of
Privileges under Rule 226 of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly
Rules, for examination and report.
2. The Committee of Privileges met on 05.05.2003 to examine the
news items, articles and editorials in question, and formed the
opinion that certain statements contained therein constituted,
prima facie , a breach of privilege. Notices were, accordingly,
issued to the petitioners, calling upon them to appear before the
Committee on 12.05.2003 and to furnish their explanation. The
petitioners appeared before the Committee and sought time to submit
their written explanation.
1

--- Page 51 ---
3. It appears that, even before the petitioners could appear
before the House, the Legislative Assembly, by a resolution dated
07.11.2003, held the publications in question to constitute a gross
contempt of the House and a breach of its privileges, and sentenced
the petitioners to simple imprisonment for a period of fifteen
days.
4. It is this action of the State Legislative Assembly that is
assailed in the present writ petitions.
5. By  an  order  dated  08.12.2003,  this  Court  noted  that
substantial questions of law arose for consideration in these
proceedings, touching upon the interpretation of Articles 194(3),
19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution, the interplay between Articles
194(3) and 19(1)(a), and the interpretation of other provisions of
the Constitution. The matter was, accordingly, referred to a Five-
Judge Bench.
6. In the interregnum, the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly passed
another resolution on 30.07.2004. The relevant portion thereof has
been extracted in the affidavit dated 24.08.2004 filed by Mr. V.
Rajaraman,  the  then  Secretary  of  the  Tamil  Nadu  Legislative
Assembly, which reads as follows:
“II.  I state that the resolution passed by the Tamil
Nadu Legislative Assembly reads as under:
“Extract of the Government Resolution passed by the
Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly on 30.7.2004”
2

--- Page 52 ---
“While publishing the proceedings of the House, the
Press,  in  the  interest  of  the  State  and  in  the
interest of the people, should be neutral and publish
the actual version of the report without giving room
for any personal bias.  The rules and guidelines of
the House are only to prevent the publication, by any
newspaper, of false and distorted news relating to the
proceedings of the Assembly.  If it is not ensured,
the public could be misled leading to undesirable
conclusions.  Therefore, in the hope that the Press
and the visual media will unflinchingly adhere to this
essential principle which is valid for all time, and
in the hope that “The Hindu” and other dailies would
publish true and faithful report of the proceedings of
the Assembly keeping in view the prestige, dignity and
privileges of the House, I move that the resolutions
passed  by  the  House  on  07.11.2003  based  on  the
recommendations of the Committee of Privileges in the
Privilege  issue  against  “The  Hindu”  and  other
newspapers be cancelled and that all the actions taken
against “The Hindu” and other dailies on the basis of
those resolutions be dropped.”
7. It,  however,  appears  that  this  significant  subsequent
development, whereby the Legislative Assembly unanimously resolved
to withdraw its earlier resolution dated 07.11.2003 against the
petitioners, escaped the notice of this Court. Thus, on 08.12.2004,
without the benefit of this development, this Court noted that
certain observations in Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha &
Ors., 1959 Supp. (1) SCR 806, a decision of a Five-Judge Bench,
appeared to be in conflict with the exposition of the powers,
privileges and immunities of State Legislatures in  Re: Special
Reference No. 1 of 1964 , (1965) 1 SCR 413, a decision of a Seven-
Judge Bench, notwithstanding that the latter had expressed its
agreement with  Pandit M.S.M. Sharma  (supra). In view of this
3

--- Page 53 ---
apparent inconsistency, the matter was referred to a Seven-Judge
Bench.
8. It is in this backdrop that the matter has now come up before
us.
9. At the outset, Mr. Raju Ramachandran, learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, invited our
attention to the affidavit dated 24.08.2004 filed by the then
Secretary of the Assembly, which places on record the subsequent
unanimous resolution of the Assembly dated 30.07.2004.
10. In view of the said resolution, whereby the earlier resolution
dated 07.11.2003 stands withdrawn, learned Senior Counsel for the
petitioners, the learned Attorney General for India and Mr. Raju
Ramachandran, learned Senior Counsel for the Tamil Nadu Legislative
Assembly, are ad idem that the present petitions have been rendered
infructuous and that no cause of action survives for adjudication.
11. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners, however, drew our
attention to the order dated 08.12.2004 and submitted that several
substantial  questions  of  law  would  otherwise  arise  for
consideration. It was further submitted, and rightly so, that the
important questions of law adverted to by this Court in the said
order  ought,  in  the  circumstances,  to  be  left  open  for
consideration in an appropriate proceeding. We find merit in this
submission.
4

--- Page 54 ---
12. Accordingly, the present writ petitions are disposed of as
having been rendered infructuous. The questions of law arising for
consideration are, however, left open to be adjudicated by this
Court in an appropriate proceeding as and when the occasion arises.
13. Pending application(s), if any, including application(s) for
intervention, stand closed.

REPORTABLE 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.     OF 2026 
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.7334/2026)  
 
 
DANISH & ORS.  ..... APPELLANT(S) 
   
               
               VERSUS 
  
   
STATE OF UP & ANR.  ..... RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
1. Leave granted.  
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.  
3. Appellants are aggrieved by order dated 
30.10.2025, passed by the High Court of Judicature at 
Allahabad (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) 
whereby the order of the learned Sessions Judge 
rejecting the prayer of the  second respondent for 
consolidation of the two cases was set aside with a 
further direction to consolidate the two cases.  
4. Before we advert to the two orders, it would be 
appropriate to briefly narrate the relevant facts.  
5. As per FIR dated 01.07.2021 lodged by one Irfan, 

--- Page 61 ---
2 
i.e., father of the first appellant, the accused 
persons, namely, Jamshed, Pappu, Amir, Sahil, Sahib, 
Suhaib and Sattar, trespassed into their house. They 
were armed with sharp edged weapons, sticks, danda, 
tabal and knife. They indiscriminately attacked the 
inmates of the house and the two sons of the informant; 
Danish and Aamir sustained serious injuries in their 
head and suffered fracture on the bones. 
6. This FIR was registered by the Baraut Police 
Station as Case Crime No.759 of 2021 under Sections 
147, 148, 149, 323, 308, 354, 354-B, and 506 of the 
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).  
7. Five days later, i.e., on 06.07.2021, Sameena, 
wife of Momin, lodged a complaint before the Chief 
Judicial Magistrate at Baghpat naming the following 
persons as accused: Danish, Aamir, Irfan, Gulfam, 
Javed and Arshad. 
8. In the complaint, it was stated that at about 10:00 
PM of 01.07.2021, the accused persons forcibly entered 
into her house carrying iron rods, firearms and 
knives. They started abusing the inmates and assaulted 
the complainant and her husband. 
9. It may be mentioned that Case Crime No.759 of 2021 

--- Page 62 ---
3 
has since been registered as Sessions Trial No.344 of 
2022 on the file of Additional Sessions Judge/Fast 
Track Court No.1, Baghpat under Sections 147, 148, 
149, 452, 323, 504, 506, 354, 324, 325 and 301 IPC. 
On the other hand, the complaint was registered as 
Complaint Case No.5725 of 2021 before the Court of 
Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Baghpat under 
Sections 147, 148, 452, 324, 323 and 506 IPC.  
10. In Sessions Trial No.344 of 2022, respondent No.2 
filed an application for clubbing of the Complaint 
Case No. 5725 of 2021 with the aforesaid case.  
11. However, learned Additional Sessions Judge vide 
the order dated 09.09.2025 took the view that the later 
complaint is not a cross case; therefore, he rejected 
the prayer for consolidation. 
12. Against this order, the second respondent moved an 
application before the High Court under Section 528 
of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (for 
short, ‘BNSS’). High Court recorded that learned 
counsel for both the parties agreed on one point that 
the incidents arising out of Case Crime No.759 of 2021 
and Complaint Case No.5725 of 2021 are the same and 
occurred at the same time as well as both the parties 

--- Page 63 ---
4 
sustained injuries. 
13. Considering the above, the High Court vide the 
order dated 30.10.2025 set aside the order of the 
learned Additional Sessions Judge dated 09.09.2025 and 
directed that Complaint Case No.5725 of 2021 be 
consolidated with Sessions Trial No.344 of 2022 and 
tried together. 
14. It is this order which is in impugnment in the 
present appeal. 
15. This Court vide the order dated 21.04.2026 had 
issued notice and stayed the impugned order of the 
High Court dated 30.10.2025 as well as further 
proceedings in Complaint Case No.5725 of 2021 and 
Sessions Trial No.344 of 2022. 
16. Learned counsel for the appellants submits that in 
so far Sessions Trial No.344 of 2022 is concerned, the 
same is now at the final stage of arguments. It is an 
attempt by the accused persons to delay the 
proceedings by getting the complaint case consolidated 
with the sessions case. He also submits that situs of 
the two incidents though may be in the near vicinity 
of each other, nonetheless, these are two separate 
incidents. The fact that the complaint was lodged 5 

--- Page 64 ---
5 
days after lodging of the FIR itself indicates that 
it is certainly not a cross case. He further submits 
that appellants have taken steps against the learned 
counsel who had represented them before the High Court 
as they had not consented to consolidation. He has 
also placed reliance on a judgment of this Court in 
the case of Lakshmanan vs. State reported in 2025 SCC 
OnLine 2889. He, therefore, submits that the impugned 
order of the High Court should be set aside and the 
Sessions Trial may be allowed to proceed unhindered 
by consolidation with the complaint case. 
17. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent 
No.2 strenuously argued that notwithstanding the delay 
in lodging of the complaint, it is evident that the 
two incidents leading to lodging of the FIR and the 
compliant are connected with each other. He has 
extensively referred to the proceedings before the 
courts including that of the High Court to contend 
that it was on a concession by the learned counsel for 
the appellants that the High Court directed 
consolidation. No prejudice will be caused to the 
appellants if both the cases are tried together. As a 
matter of fact, after the impugned order was passed 
by the High Court, the complaint case has also been 

--- Page 65 ---
6 
placed before the same Court to be tried as a sessions 
case being Sessions Case No.144 of 2026. 
18. On the other hand, Mr. Bansal, learned State 
counsel  submits that it would be beneficial for both 
the sides if there is a joint trial. Further, the Court 
would be benefited by the deposition of the witnesses 
who would be  more or less common in both the 
proceedings. He, therefore, submits that the impugned 
order passed by the High Court is just and proper and 
no interference is called for. 
19. Submissions made by learned counsel for the 
parties have received the due consideration of the 
Court. 
20. We have already noticed the facts leading to 
registration of the FIR and the complaint. We have 
also noted that while according to the appellants, the 
accused persons (represented by the second respondent) 
had trespassed into their residence and had assaulted 
them, as per the version of the second respondent, the 
accused persons (represented by the appellants herein) 
had forcibly entered into their residence and had 
assaulted him and others. While the time of the 
incident mentioned in the FIR is from 8:00 PM to 10:30 

--- Page 66 ---
7 
PM on 01.07.2021, the time mentioned in the complaint 
is about 10:00 PM of the same day. No doubt, the two 
alleged incidents occurred in close proximity of each 
other but the situs of the two incidents are different. 
The FIR refers to the trespass and assault in the 
residence of the appellants whereas the complaint 
refers to trespass and assault in the residence of the 
second respondent. That apart, we have noticed that 
neither the complainant i.e. Sameena nor her husband 
i.e. Momin have been named as accused in the FIR. 
21. Sub-section (1) of Section 218 CrPC says that for 
every distinct offence of which any person is accused, 
there shall be a separate charge and every such charge 
shall be tried separately. As per the proviso, where 
the accused person makes an application in writing and 
the Magistrate is of the opinion that such person is 
not likely to be produced, the Magistrate may try 
together or any number of the charges framed against 
such person. Therefore, under Section 218(1) CrPC, 
separate trial in each distinct offence against the 
same accused is the norm. 
22. As per sub-section (1) of Section 219 CrPC, when 
a person is accused of more offences than one of the 
same kind committed within a space of 12 months from 

--- Page 67 ---
8 
the first to the last of such offences, whether in 
respect of the same person or not, he may be charged 
with and tried at one trial for the offences but the 
number of such offences should not exceed three. 
23. Similarly, under Section 220(1) CrPC, if in one 
series of acts so connected together to form the same 
transaction, more offences than one are committed by 
the same person, he may be charged with and tried at 
one trial for every such offence.  
24. Sections 221 and 222 CrPC deal with different 
variants of charges arising out of a single act or a 
series of acts resulting in such offences. Section 223 
CrPC provides that the persons named thereunder may 
be charged and tried together, such as, persons 
accused of the same offence committed in the course 
of the same transaction; persons accused of an offence 
and persons accused of an abetment or attempt to commit 
such offence etc.    
25. The law relating to consolidation, whether it is 
a sessions triable case and a complaint case, has been 
gone into in detail by this Court in Lakshmanan. It 
is not necessary to refer to the various provisions 
of law and the analysis made by the Bench in 

--- Page 68 ---
9 
Lakshmanan. In paragraph 13.3, this Court summed up 
as under: 
(i) Separate trial is the rule under 
Section 218 Cr.P.C.; a joint trial may be 
permissible where the offences form part 
of the same transaction or the conditions 
in Sections 219-223 Cr.P.C. are 
satisfied, but even then it is a matter 
of judicial discretion; 
(ii) The decision to hold a joint or 
separate trial must ordinarily be taken 
at the outset of the proceedings and for 
cogent reasons; 
(iii) The two paramount considerations in 
such decision making are whether a joint 
trial would cause prejudice to the 
accused, and whether it would occasion 
delay or wastage of judicial time. 
26. Finally we note that one is a sessions triable case 
having serious consequences and the other is a 
complaint case ordinarily adjudicated by a court 
placed lower in the hierarchy. In such a situation, 
we are of the view that clubbing of the two proceedings 
is really not warranted. The High Court committed an 
error in interfering with the order passed by the 
learned Additional Sessions Judge dated 09.09.2025 and 
directing consolidation. 

--- Page 69 ---
10 
27. For all the aforesaid reasons, we set aside the 
impugned order of the High Court dated 30.10.2025 and 
direct that both the two cases being Sessions Trial 
No.344 of 2022 and Complaint Case No.5725 of 2021 shall 
be proceeded with separately before the respective 
courts in accordance with law. 
28. Appeal is accordingly allowed. 
29. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed 
of.

(UJJAL BHUYAN)

the recent natural calamity in Nepal which led to the level
of river Ganga rising has submerged this entire portion and
this made it difficult for the authorities to proceed
further with the removal of the encroachments.
4. We grant for one last time, eight weeks’ time period to
comply with our directions, failing which, we shall have to

summon the Chief Secretary of the State of Bihar and other
authorities before us and we may also proceed further with
contempt.

intervenors  to  prefer  an  appropriate  representation

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.351/2013
BANDU RAMCHANDRA SHINDE & ORS.    Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
We have heard the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the appellants and the learned
counsel appearing for the respondent-State.
The appellants before us, A-2, A-3 and A-4
were convicted for the offences punishable under
Sections 302 read with Section 149; Section 307
read with Section 149; Section 148 and Section
147 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short
‘IPC’) and were sentenced to undergo imprisonment
for  life  by  the  Trial  Court.   The  appeals
preferred by them before the High Court also came
to be dismissed. Aggrieved, the present appeals
have been preferred.

--- Page 107 ---
2
The case of the prosecution, in a nutshell,
is that on 28.11.2001, on account of enmity
between the deceased and the accused persons, the
accused  persons  formed  an  unlawful  assembly,
attacked the deceased, assaulted the complainant
and committed the offence.  Consequently, Case
Crime  No.147/2001  was  registered  against  the
accused person.
The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
appellants submit that the issue involved in the
present case is no longer res integra, as in a
similar case, being Rafiq Burhan Shaikh & Anr. v.
The  State  of  Maharashtra  -  Criminal  Appeal
Nos.1852-1853/2011 dated 11.09.2024, this Court
was pleased to modify the conviction to one
punishable under Section 307, IPC along with
other provisions, while acquitting the appellants
therein under Section 302, IPC by taking note of
the fact that there was no specific overt act
attributed as against them and the accused person
who was primarily responsible for the death of

--- Page 108 ---
3
the victim subsequently died.
It is further submitted that in the present
case also, the main accused, namely, A-1 who is
said to have attacked the deceased and caused
death, is no more.  Insofar as the appellants
before us are concerned, they allegedly attacked
the complainant alone.
On a query, the learned counsel appearing
for the respondent submits that it is true that
the facts involved in the present appeal are
similar to the ones involved in  Rafiq Burhan
Shaikh & Anr. (supra) dated 11.09.2024.  However,
in any case, the charge under Section 307, IPC
would continue.
We have perused the evidence available on
record,  especially  the  statement  of  the
complainant and the one made by PWs 10, 14, 16
and 18.
Considering  the  above,  particularly,  the
overt  act  attributed  against  the  appellants,
coupled with the fact that A-1, who attacked the

--- Page 109 ---
4
deceased and caused death is no more; and after
verifying the relevant record, we find that the
punishment imposed under Section 302 read with
Section 149, IPC will have to be set aside.
Further, the High Court convicted only three
persons out of the total ten accused persons, so,
the charge under Section 149 of the IPC shall not
be made out.
Furthermore, we have been informed that two
of  the  appellants  have  already  undergone
incarceration of 10 years each and one appellant
has undergone incarceration of seven and a half
years.
In  such  view  of  the  matter,  while
maintaining the conviction under Section 307,
IPC, we are inclined to modify the sentence of
the appellants to the one they have already
undergone.
Accordingly, the impugned order passed by
the High Court confirming that of the Trial Court
stands modified.  The appellants are acquitted of

--- Page 110 ---
5
all other charges except one punishable under
Section 307, IPC. The sentences imposed on the
appellants stand modified to the one already
undergone by them. 
Bail bonds stand discharged, accordingly.
The appeal stands allowed, in part.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of. 
………………………………………………….J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
………………………………………………….J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]
NEW DELHI;
OCTOBER 08, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) NO. 16173/2026)
JASVIR SINGH              Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB                         Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 04.08.2026
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Punjab  and  Haryana  at
Chandigarh in CRM-M-32274-2026 (O&M). 
This Criminal Appeal arises out of crime registered
pursuant to FIR No.303/2025 dated 18.12.2025 lodged with
Police  Station  Sadar,  Ludhiana,  District  Police
Commissionerate Ludhiana under Sections 115(2), 117(1),
126(2), 351(2), 191(3), 125, 190, 109 and 238 of Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (‘BNS’) and under Sections 25 and 27
of the Arms Act, 1959. The appellant was taken into
custody  in  connection  with  the  aforesaid  crime  on
20.12.2025. The appellant preferred CRM-M-32274-2026 (O&M)
before  the  High  Court  of  Punjab  and  Haryana  seeking
regular bail. 
The application seeking regular bail having been
rejected  by  the  High  Court  by  impugned  order  dated
04.08.2026, the present appeal has been preferred. 

--- Page 126 ---
2
By order dated 07.09.2026, this Court issued notice
in the instant matter.
We have heard learned senior counsel in support of
the appellant and learned AAG for the respondent-state. 
Learned senior counsel for the appellant submitted
that this is a case of political rivalry; that in fact the
appellant herein merely acted in self-defence and the
gunshot accidentally hit the injured; in fact the opposite
party had also proceeded as an armed mob intending to kill
the  appellant’s  son.  Furthermore,  no  case  has  been
registered as against the opposite party. Moreover, five
out of eight co-accused have already been enlarged on
bail;  the  chargesheet  has  been  filed  as  against  the
appellant herein. In the circumstances, this Court may set
aside the impugned order and grant the relief of bail to
the appellant herein subject to the terms and conditions
to be imposed. 
Per contra, learned AAG appearing for the State of
Punjab refuted these contentions and stated that the
allegations as against the appellant herein are serious;
it is not a case of self-defence at all; there was an
intention on the part of the appellant to use his firearm
against  the  members  of  the  opposite  party.  In  the
circumstances, this Court may simply dismiss this appeal.

--- Page 127 ---
3
In  response  to  this  submission,  learned  senior
counsel for the appellant contended that insofar as the
opposite  party  is  concerned,  there  has  been  no  FIR
registered  as  against  them  at  the  instance  of  the
appellant. This itself shows that the State is not acting
in a fair manner. In the circumstances, the relief of bail
may granted to the appellant herein.
Considering the facts on record, in our view, the
case for regular bail is made out. 
We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as under:
“The appellant Jasvir Singh shall be produced
before the concerned Trial Court as early as
possible and the Court shall release him on bail
in the proceedings arising out of Sadar, Ludhiana
P.S. FIR No. 303/2025, subject to such conditions
as it may deem appropriate to impose to ensure his
presence in the proceedings arising out of the
concerned FIR mentioned above.”
It  is  directed  that  the  appellant  shall  extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing trial. 
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and shall
not in any way influence the witnesses or tamper with the
material on record. 

--- Page 128 ---
4
Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may  entail
cancellation of bail granted to the appellant.
With the aforesaid directions, the Criminal Appeal is
allowed.
…………………………………………………J.
                                    ( B.V. NAGARATHNA )

O R D E R
1. These two contempt petitions have been filed alleging willful
disobedience of the order dated 29.01.2025 passed by this Court in
Special  Leave  Petition  (Civil)  Nos.28876/2016  and  2670/2025  and
other  connected  Special  Leave  Petition  (Civil)  No.5405/2023.  On
notice  being  issued of alleged contempt, compliance  affidavit has
been filed by the respondents stating thereunder that judgment /
order  /  directions  issued  by  this  Court  has  been  complied  with.
However, the learned Senior Counsels appearing for the petitioners –
complainants would vehemently contend that order passed by this
Court has not been complied in letter and spirit and as such there is
willful disobedience.
1

--- Page 138 ---
2. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties, we
are of the considered view that it would be apt and appropriate to
extract the actual direction issued by this Court vide  order dated
29.01.2025 which is alleged to have been willfully disobeyed and it
reads thus:
“12. In view of the foregoing, this Court has accepted
the view taken by the Calcutta High Court in the case of the
other  Tower  Wagon  Drivers  i.e.,  WPCT  No.  70  of  2007
Union of India v. Ram Chandra & Ors.  and that of the
High Court of Orissa, Cuttack in WP(C) No. 14082 of 2024
titled Union of India and ors. v. Sanjay Kumar and Ors.
Therefore, there is no reason to take a different view in this
case. Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High
Court is set aside. The petitioners would be entitled to get all
benefits, as allowed by the High Court of Calcutta in the case
of W.P.C.T. No. 70/2007 titled Union of India & Ors. v. Ram
Chandra & Ors  and High Court of Orissa, Cuttack in WP(C)
No. 14082 of 2024 titled Union of India and ors. v. Sanjay
Kumar and Ors.”
3. A  perusal  of  the  aforesaid  order  would  clearly  indicate  that
respondents  therein  were  directed  to  comply  with  the  directions
which have been issued by the High Court of Calcutta in the case of
W.P.C.T.  No.70/2007  titled  as  Union  of  India  &  Ors.  Vs.  Ram
Chandra  &  Ors. and  High  Court  of  Orissa,  Cuttack  in  W.P.  (C)
No.14082/2024 titled as Union of India & Ors. Vs. Sanjay Kumar
& Ors. The said judgment is also available on the file of the present
case. Suffice to state or extract the judgment of High Court of Orissa
rendered in W.P. (C) No.14082/2024 and it reads as under:
“7.    The Tribunal, after due adjudication, came to a definite
finding  that  as  to  whether  the  Tower  Wagon  Drivers  are
entitled  to  Running  Allowance,  as  was  given  to  the  Goods
Drivers, was the subject matter of consideration before the
apex  Court  in  Civil  Appeal  No.365  of  2007,  which  was
ultimately set at rest in favour of the Tower Wagon Drivers
vide  order  dated  08.07.2010.  The  Tribunal,  relying  upon
2

--- Page 139 ---
paragraphs 5, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of the said Civil Appeal,
quashed the orders dated 20.06.2016 and 26.05.2016 passed
by petitioner no.3, rejecting the representation of the opposite
parties and intimating that they are not entitled for grant of
pay  scale  of  Rs.5000-8000/-  at  par  with  Goods  drivers
respectively, and directed the petitioners to fix the pay of the
opposite  parties  in  the  pay  scale  of  Rs.1350-2200/-  w.e.f.
01.01.1986  and  Rs.5000-8000/- w.e.f.  01.01.1996  notionally
and with effect from the date of filing the aforesaid O.A. w.e.f.
July, 2016 and complete the entire exercise within a period of
180 days from the date of receipt of the copy of the order.
Therefore, this Court is not inclined to take a different view
than the view taken by the Tribunal.” 
4. The direction issued in the aforesaid judgment is to the effect
that contemnors are required to pay the writ applicants the pay-scale
of Rs.1350-2200/- with effect from 01.01.1986 and Rs.5000-8000/-
with effect from 01.01.1996 notionally and with effect from the date
of the filing of the aforesaid O.A., i.e., with effect from July, 2016 and
were also directed to complete the entire exercise within a period of
180 days from the date of the receipt of the copy of the order. This
direction issued by the Orissa High Court has been juxtapositioned in
the order dated 29.01.2025 passed by this Court and the respondents
herein have been directed to comply with the directions issued by the
Calcutta High Court and the Orissa High Court.
5. In the aforesaid background, when the compliance affidavit is
perused,  it  would  clearly  indicate  that  in  paragraph  No.10  of  the
compliance affidavit, it is specifically stated that with the approval of
the competent authority, the benefit of pay-scale of Rs.5000-8000 (GP
– 4200 / Level-6) has been granted to the applicants notionally with
effect from 01.01.1996; actually with effect from 28.02.2012 (date of
filing of the Original Application) and the competent authority vide its
3

--- Page 140 ---
communication dated 24.09.2025 had approved the pay-fixation of
the petitioner in O.A. No.631/2012 and granted the benefits of the
said pay-scale. Paragraph No.12 of the complaince affidavit would
also  indicate  that  competent  authority  vide  communication  dated
12.03.2026 has issued revised Pension Payment Orders in respect of
all  the  applicants  and  revised  the  dues  and  have  released  the
amounts  accordingly.  However,  for  the  procedural  delay,  an
unconditional apology has been tendered.
6. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner  in  Contempt
Petition No.734/2025 (Serial No.48.1) would contend that the order of
this Court dated 29.01.2025 is clear and explicit, namely, this Court
has directed the contemnors to compute the amounts payable with
effect from the date of filing of the O.A. and he would contend that
O.A. No.1699/2000 was filed in the year 2000 itself and the order of
the Central Administrative Tribunal dated 27.01.2003 was affirmed by
jurisdictional High court in W.P. (C) No.6925/2010 and there being no
further appeal against the said orders, the respondents – contemnors
cannot take an umbrage under the subsequent order of the Central
Administrative Tribunal for purposes of computation. Subsequent to
this  order  of  10.11.2010,  a  notification  came  to  be  issued  on
15.11.2010  which  constrained  the  complainants  to  file  fresh  O.A.
No.631/2012 which reached finality upto this Court by order dated
29.01.2025. If the authorities have understood that on subsequent
passing of the notification if gave birth to fresh cause of action for
4

--- Page 141 ---
seeking disparity in the pay and that has been negatived and the
authorities have implemented the subsequent order of O.A., it cannot
be  gainsaid  by  the  complainants  that  there  has  been  willful
disobedience of the order of this Court. As such reserving liberty to
the complainants to challenge as to the date of entitlement namely
whether it would be from the date of the filing of the first O.A., i.e.,
1699/2000 or from the filing of the second O.A., i.e., 631/2012 the
present contempt proceedings stands closed.
7. In view of the above, we are of the considered view that there is
no willful disobedience of the order dated 29.01.2025 passed by this
Court. Hence, the contempt proceedings stands closed. However we
grant liberty  to  the  petitioners  to  challenge  the  Pension  Payment
Orders. if so advised and if being aggrieved by the same. Accordingly,
the Contempt Petitions stand disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

A. The Union of India shall, if not

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant has been convicted under Section 302 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) by the
1

--- Page 161 ---
Sessions Judge, Ganjam-Gajapati, Berhampur, Odisha in
Sessions Trial Case No.427 of 2009 and sentenced to
undergo Imprisonment for Life.
4. Appeal  filed  by  the  appellant  against  his
conviction and sentence was rejected by the High
Court of Orissa at Cuttack (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter),  vide  the  judgment  and  order  dated
29.07.2022.
5. On the basis of custody certificate, it can be
seen that as of now, appellant has undergone actual
incarceration of about 17 years.
6. On  07.09.2026,  we  had  issued  notice  on  the
Special Leave Petition as well as on the prayer for
bail.
7. This Court, in the case of In Re: Policy Strategy
for Grant of Bail [2025 SCC OnLine SC 349],  recorded
the following conclusions:
“21.  We,  therefore,  record  the  following
conclusions:
a) Where  there  is  a  policy  of  the
appropriate Government laying down guidelines
for consideration of the grant of premature
release under Section 432 of the CrPC or
Section 473 of the BNSS, it is the obligation
of the appropriate Government to consider
cases of all convicts for grant of premature
release as and when they become eligible for
consideration in terms of the policy. In such
a case, it is not necessary for the convict
or  his  relatives  to  make  a  specific
application for grant of permanent remission.
2

--- Page 162 ---
When  the  jail  manual  or  any  other
departmental  instruction  issued  by  the
appropriate Government contains such policy
guidelines,  the  aforesaid  direction  will
apply;
b) We  direct  those  States  and  Union
Territories that do not have a policy dealing
with the grant of remission in terms of
Section 432 of the CrPC or Section 473 of the
BNSS to formulate a policy within two months
from today;
c) Appropriate Government has the power to
incorporate suitable conditions in an order
granting permanent remission. Consideration
of various factors, which are mentioned in
paragraph 13 above by way of illustration, is
necessary before finalizing the conditions.
The conditions must aim at ensuring that the
criminal tendencies, if any, of the convict
remain  in  check  and  that  the  convict
rehabilitates himself in the society. The
conditions should not be so oppressive or
stringent that the convict is not able to
take  advantage  of  the  order  granting
permanent remission. The conditions cannot be
vague  and  should  be  capable  of  being
performed;
d) Order granting or refusing the relief of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons. The order containing reasons should
be immediately communicated to the convict
through the office of the concerned prison.
The copies thereof should be forwarded to the
Secretaries of the concerned District Legal
Services Authorities. It is the duty of the
prison authorities to inform the convict that
he has the right to challenge the order of
rejection of the prayer for the grant of
remission.
3

--- Page 163 ---
e) As held in the case of Mafabhai Motibhai
Sagar, an order granting permanent remission
cannot  be  withdrawn  or  cancelled  without
giving an opportunity of being heard to the
convict.  An  order  of  cancellation  of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons;
f) The District Legal Services Authorities
shall endeavour to implement NALSA SOP in its
true letter and spirit.
g) Further,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall also monitor implementation
of conclusion (a) as recorded above. For this
purpose,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall maintain the relevant date
of the convicts and as and when they become
eligible to a consideration for grant of
premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal
Services  Authorities  shall  endeavour  to
create  a  portal  on  which  the  data  as
aforesaid  can  be  uploaded  on  real  time
basis.”
8. In terms of Paragraph 21(g) of the conclusions
extracted  herein  above,  District  Legal  Services
Authorities  have  been  mandated  to  monitor
implementation of conclusion (a). For this purpose,
the  District  Legal  Services  Authorities  shall
maintain the relevant data of the convicts and as and
when they become eligible for a consideration for
grant of premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal Services
Authorities shall endeavour to create a portal on
4

--- Page 164 ---
which the data as aforesaid can be uploaded on real
time basis.
9. We, therefore, direct the appropriate Government,
i.e. State of Odisha, to consider the case for
permanent remission of the appellant as per the
applicable remission policy.
10. The  District  Legal  Services  Authority  of
Berhampur shall do the needful so that the remission
papers of the appellant can be transmitted to the
State Government for necessary consideration.
11. In  view  of  the  long  incarceration  of  the
appellant, we direct, as an interim measure, that the
appellant shall be released on bail from jail on
usual terms and conditions.
12. Interim bail granted to the appellant shall not
be taken as a factor against the appellant while
considering his case for permanent remission.
13. Let the consideration be carried out within 03
months from today.
14. List the matter after 03 months.
(ABHINAV KUMAR)                                (CHETNA BALOONI)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
     CIVIL APPEAL NOS.          /2026
    [@ SLP (C) NOS.10758-10759/2026]
M/S A.S. CARRIERS PVT. LTD.               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE INDUSTRIES PROMOTION 
CORPORATION OF TAMIL NADU LTD Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeals have been filed challenging
the impugned judgment passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Madras in Writ Appeal Nos. 2043/2023
and 920/2023, whereby, the learned Division Bench
upheld  the  levy  of  sub-leasing  charges  by  the
respondent-SIPCOT, by allowing the writ appeal filed
by the respondent.  Initially, the writ petition was
filed  by  the  appellant  seeking  to  quash  the
communication  dated  28.04.2014,  wherein,  the
respondent issued a demand against the appellant to
remit  a  sum  of  Rs.5,09,52,037/-  along  with  the
Service Tax at the rate of 12.36%, within a period of
90 days.
3. The  learned  Single  Judge  allowed  the  writ
petition, by holding that there was no clause as per
the lease deed which authorized the respondent to

--- Page 171 ---
2
demand  sub-lease  charges  unilaterally,  when
warehousing facilities were let out to third parties.
The  learned  Single  Judge  further  relied  upon  a
clarificatory letter issued by the respondent dated
14.10.2004,  which  made  it  permissible  for  the
appellant  to  lease  warehousing  and  logistic
facilities developed by it.  It was further observed
that the appropriate remedy in violation of terms of
lease deed, would have been to cancel the allotment
order itself, and not that of raising a unilateral
demand.
4. Aggrieved,  the  respondent  preferred  a  writ
appeal before the Division Bench.  The same was
allowed by holding that the conditions stipulated in
Clause 39 of the lease deed must be read in the
context of the Public Trust Doctrine.  It was further
held that Clause 39 empowered the respondent to
impose any further conditions and stipulations or
alterations in the regulations, necessary at any time
for  the  establishment  or  for  benefit  of  the
Industrial Park.   Additionally, it was held that the
appellant's action amounted to unjust enrichment, as
it was paying an annual rent of only Rs.1/- for the
entire property, whose portions were sub-leased to
third parties for much higher commercial gains. It

--- Page 172 ---
3
was accordingly held that the appellant is liable to
pay sub-leasing changes in terms of Clause 39 of the
agreement.
5. Aggrieved, the appellant is before this Court.
6. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the parties.
7. We are inclined to interfere with the impugned
order only on a limited ground as the appellant-
company was admittedly not heard before passing the
order/letter of demand dated 28.04.2014, based upon
the factual premise. Certainly the said order has got
its own consequences.
8. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
set aside the impugned order passed by the High Court
as well  as the  order raising  demand of  Rs.5.09
Crores, on the factual premise that the properties in
question have been put on sub-lease.
9. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order(s)  and  the
order/letter of demand dated 28.04.2014 raised by the
respondent  stand  set  aside.   The  respondent  is
granted liberty to issue a fresh show cause notice,
prior to raising any such demand(s), based upon which
any purported action is sought to be taken against
the appellant.
10. All the issues are left open.

--- Page 173 ---
4
11. The appeals stand allowed, accordingly.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
…………………………………………..J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
…………………………………………..J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]

1. Leave granted.

pursuant to the summoning order dated 11.11.2022.
4. Allegation of the appellant is that the cheques
issued by the first respondent were dishonoured. The
cheques were signed on behalf of the first respondent by
the second respondent being the Managing Director and an
authorised signatory of the first respondent. In so far
respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 are concerned, it was averred
that they were directors of the first respondent company
1

--- Page 176 ---
looking after the day to day affairs of the said company.
They had played a definite role leading to supply of the
goods in question by the appellant for which the cheques
(four in number) were issued which were subsequently
dishonoured. At this stage it may be mentioned that
though statutory notice was issued by the appellant to
respondent Nos. 2 to 5, there was no response.
5. Respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 thereafter moved the High
Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter) under Section 482 of the Code
of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, ‘Cr.PC’) for
quashing of the complaint. 
6. The High Court in para 6 of the impugned order dated
03.02.2025 noted that respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 appeared
to be directors of the first respondent but the cheques
were issued under the signature of the Managing Director
Arvinder  Pal  Singh.  Holding  that  the  doctrine  of
vicarious liability is a civil concept and that extension
of such a concept to criminal cases is an exception
rather  than  the  rule,  the  High  Court  quashed  the
complaint qua respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5.
7. This Court by order dated 17.09.2025 recorded the
following:
Delay condoned.
Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner
submitted that the findings recorded by the
High  Court  in  the  impugned  order  are
erroneous. It is evident from Annexure P-5,
2

--- Page 177 ---
the financial statement of the respondent
company. It shows that the respondent No.1
was drawing Director’s remuneration and also
taking  loans  from  the  company.  She  has
further  referred  to  Annexure  P-4  Final
Report/ Closure filed by the Police after
investigation of a complaint filed by M/s
Bird Machine Company against the petitioner
in which respondent No.1 - Prabh Jyoti Singh
had mentioned himself to be the Managing
Director.
As far as, Sandeep Singh is concerned, he
was  also  drawing  remuneration  from  the
company as Director.
Issue notice to the respondents returnable
on 17.11.2025.
8. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  has  drawn  the
attention  of  the  court  to  the  salary  statement  of
respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 (page 58 of the SLP paperbook)
and submits that their remuneration was even higher than
the  Managing  Director  and  other  regular  directors.
According to her, respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 are involved
in the day to day functioning of the first respondent and
their role in the management of the first respondent
cannot be extricated at the threshold without being
subjected to the rigours of the trial.
9. Per contra learned counsel appearing for respondent
Nos. 3, 4 and 5 submits that the view taken by the High
Court  is  correct.  Merely  because  remuneration  of
respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 is higher than the other
3

--- Page 178 ---
directors, it would not imply that they are incharge of
the first respondent company.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that whether
respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 are involved in the day to day
affairs of the first respondent company is a matter of
trial; a definite finding can be reached only after
considering  the  evidence  by  the  Trial  Magistrate.
Therefore,  the  High  Court  was  not  justified  in
terminating the proceedings under Section 138 of the NI
Act qua respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 at the threshold.
11. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of the
High Court dated 03.02.2025 and direct that all the
respondents would be subjected to the trial proceedings.
12. We, however, make it clear that we have not expressed
any opinion on merit and all contentions are kept open.
13. Appeals are accordingly allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

 1                                                                              SLP(CRL.) NO.4899 OF 2026

--- Page 191 ---
4. It is not in dispute that there is a civil suit also

the custodial interrogation of the appellant would not be

investigation.

reason.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  Appeal  has  been  filed
challenging  the  Judgment  and  Order  dated
23.01.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Chhattisgarh  whereby  the  appellant-accused’s
appeal was partly allowed. Though the conviction
was upheld, yet the sentence under Section 377
IPC and Section 6 of The Protection of Children
from  Sexual  Offences  Act,  2012  (POCSO)  was
reduced  from  life  imprisonment  to  20  years
rigorous imprisonment on the ground that the life
sentence was the maximum sentence and the same
was  disproportionate  given  the  appellant-
accused’s age and circumstances.
1

--- Page 196 ---
3. This  Court  while  issuing  notice  on
26.05.2026 had passed the following order:
“ Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner. 
2. Delay condoned.
3. At the outset, learned counsel for
the  petitioner  submitted  that  the
illegality in the sentencing is writ
large by the fact that the High Court
has come to the opinion that minimum
sentence should be awarded but still,
has proceeded to award twenty years of
rigorous  imprisonment  to  the
petitioner under Section 377 of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  and  under
Section  6  of  the  Protection  of
Children  from  Sexual  Offences  Act,
2012 (hereinafter referred to as the
“POCSO Act”). It was submitted that at
the relevant point of time, when the
alleged act was committed, the law
provided  for  minimum  ten  years  of
rigorous  imprisonment  whereas,  the
High Court has erred in taking it to
be  twenty  years  of  rigorous
imprisonment,  when  admittedly  the
minimum sentence was enhanced from ten
years to twenty years in the POCSO Act
on 16.08.2019 whereas, the incident is
alleged  to  have  occurred  on
19.04.2019.
4. Limited to the aforesaid aspect,
issue notice.
5. List on 12.08.2026.”
2

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
I.A. No…….In Writ Petition(s)(Civil) No(s).1112/2025
SHAHEEN MALIK                                 Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ANR.                              Respondent(s)
Date : 09-10-2026 This I.A. was mentioned today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Applicant(s) Ms. Kriti Mazumdar, AOR      
Mr. Ankush Kapoor, Adv.
                    Mr. Zainab Khan, Adv.
     Mr. Arnav Abhishek, Adv.
     Ms. Huda Naaz, Adv.
     Mr. Daksh Kayastha, Adv.
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. An application has been handed over in the Court today on
behalf of an acid attack victim, through Shaheen Malik, Director of
the Brave Souls Foundation, an organisation dedicated to the
rehabilitation, welfare and securing of justice for acid attack
survivors. 
2. It  was  brought  to  our  notice  that  the  victim  was
allegedly attacked on 06.10.2026 at about 6:30 AM at Gondha Chowk,
Bhajanpura, Delhi, in respect of which FIR No. 424/2026 was
registered at Police Station Bhajanpura on the same day. In her
statement recorded in the FIR, the victim named Tajjudin @ Sikander
as the assailant, who is alleged to have fled the spot after the
attack. Members of the public came to her aid and a call was made

--- Page 205 ---
2
to the emergency helpline number 112, whereafter she was taken by
PCR to JPC Hospital and referred from there to GTB Hospital for
further treatment.
3. It is further averred that on 08.10.2026 the victim
sought discharge from GTB Hospital and left for Sir Ganga Ram
Hospital in a private ambulance at about 3:45 PM, reaching it by
about 4:45 PM. She was allegedly refused admission and made to wait
in the ambulance until about 6:45 PM, without any medical treatment
or even a stretcher, and the hospital staff then directed that the
ambulance be removed from the waiting area as other patients were
arriving. She was allowed into the emergency ward at about 6:45 PM
only upon the intervention of counsel. 
4. Even thereafter, she and her mother were repeatedly told
that  she  would  be  discharged  with  a  referral  to  Safdarjung
Hospital, and nothing beyond first-aid dressings was administered.
On 09.10.2026, the family was asked to seek her discharge on the
ground that the hospital has no dedicated burn unit. An attempt to
approach Apollo Hospital met with a similar response, the hospital
having informed the petitioner telephonically that it has no
dedicated burn injury ward and cannot admit the victim.
5. On this basis, it is submitted that the victim has
received no effective treatment since 08.10.2026 and is in urgent
need of medical intervention at a hospital equipped to manage acid
attack and burn injuries, since any further delay carries a serious
risk of deterioration in her condition. Reliance is placed on
Section 397 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which
requires every hospital, whether public or private and whether run
by the Central Government, a State Government, a local body or any
other person, to provide first-aid medical treatment free of cost
to victims of offences covered under Section 124 of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It is urged that this obligation assumes
paramount importance in the present case, and that the victim

--- Page 206 ---
3
cannot be left without care merely because a particular hospital
lacks a specialised burn unit.
6. In light of the above alarming facts, the following
prayers have been made in the application:
“a. Direct the Respondents to forthwith ensure the
immediate  admission  and  provision  of  comprehensive
medical treatment to the acid attack victim, [xxx], at
a suitably equipped hospital having the requisite burn
unit and specialised facilities, without any further
delay or impediment; 
b. Direct the Respondents to ensure that the victim
receives all necessary medical treatment, including
emergency care, specialised burn management, surgical
intervention, medication and other requisite medical
facilities,  free  of  cost,  in  accordance  with  the
applicable provisions of law; 
c. Direct the Respondents to ensure that no hospital,
whether  public  or  private,  refuses  or  delays  the
provision of immediate medical assistance to the victim
in violation of its statutory obligations under Section
397 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023;
d. Pass such other or further orders as this Hon’ble
Court may deem fit and proper in the interest of
justice and to safeguard the life, health and dignity
of the victim”
    [Sic]
7.  At the very outset, the Registry is directed to register this
IA in WP (C) No.1112/2025.
8. In light of the serious issue and the circumstances
highlighted above, we direct the management of Sir Ganga Ram
Hospital to keep the acid attack victim ( name withheld from the
order but it will be mentioned in the order to be sent to the
hospital)  as  an  indoor  patient  and  provide  all  facilities,
including medicines and plastic surgery treatment, as and when
required, or any other treatment irrespective of the cost that has
to be incurred on such treatment.  

--- Page 207 ---
4
9. Liberty is granted to the Management of Sir Ganga Ram
Hospital to forward the bills to this Court for appropriate
directions regarding refund of the expenditure incurred by that
hospital. However, the victim shall not be discharged unless it is
certified by the doctor(s) that she is in a fit position to be
discharged and would require only outdoor treatment.
10. A copy of this order be sent to Sri Ganga Ram Hospital
today itself through fax.  
11. The  Delhi  Police  is  directed  to  arrest  the  accused
forthwith, if not already arrested and file a compliance report in
this regard. 
12. Similarly, the Superintendent of Sri Ganga Ram Hospital
shall also file a compliance report.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. In the midst of hearing of today’s matters at about 01:00
p.m., an oral mentioning was made by Mr. Kapil Sibal, Mr. Gopal
Sankaranarayanan, Mr. Hariharan N., Mr. C.U. Singh, learned senior
1

--- Page 209 ---
counsel and Ms. Vrinda Grover, Mr. Prashant Bhushan, and other
learned counsel, inter alia, pointing out two communications dated
08.10.2026 issued from the office of the Joint Commissioner of
Police, Transport Range, New Delhi to the Managing Director of the
Delhi Metro Railway Corporation (DMRC) and another communication
dated 09.10.2026, which seems to have been issued to all the zonal
railways.
2. Furthermore, a copy of the order dated 23.08.2026, issued by the
Assistant Commissioner of Police purportedly exercising authority
under Section 70 of the Delhi Police Act, 1978, and Section 163 of
the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which issues
certain prohibitory directives, was also referenced.
3. We find from the contents of the aforementioned orders that
metro trains and all Mail/Express trains arriving at New Delhi
Railway Station and Hazrat Nizamuddin Railway Station have been
instructed to cease operations or be cancelled in consideration of
the potential risk of unruly mob movements towards sensitive
locations. It is also noted that the frequency of metro trains
passing through 57 metro stations stands reduced, and their entry
and exit gates are to be closed from 9:00 p.m. on October 9, 2026,
continuing on 10.10.2026 until the situation normalizes. These
prohibitory orders have been made effective from today, that is
09.10.2026.
4. Since the subject orders referred to some proposed protestors
at Jantar Mantar, we accorded liberty to the organizers of the
protest to submit urgent petitions before this Court, as we were
inclined to accord a hearing at 2:00 PM or thereafter.
2

--- Page 210 ---
5. All the learned Senior Counsel, objecting to the cessation of
Metro and other rail services, have, however, fairly stated that
they do not represent the proposed protesters or the organizers of
the said protest. No other petition for or on their behalf has been
filed before us.
6. In light of the foregoing, the principal issue for our
consideration is whether the absolute prohibition on the movement
of Metro trains at Metro stations, as well as the movement of
trains from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin Railway Stations,
warrants reconsideration.
7. It appears that the notifications are overreaching, as they
impose a complete ban upon essential public transportation. Upon
our  indication  that  a  distinction  exists  between  total
‘prohibition’  and  the  ‘regulation’  of  Metro  and  other  train
movements, learned Solicitor General of India has fairly agreed to
impress  upon  the  authorities  to  reassess  such  prohibitions.
Consequently, they will permit the operation of Metro trains and
other  rail  services  in  such  a  regulated  manner,  that  no
inconvenience is caused to the residents and general public of
Delhi, while adhering to the principles of proportionality.
8. Regarding that assurance, we clarify that although there shall
be no outright prohibition on the movement of Metro trains, a
prudent decision may be made to permit the operation of Metro
trains and other rail services in a suitable and regulated manner.
Such a decision should be widely publicised to prevent further
inconvenience.
9. In this vein, a traffic advisory shall also be published in
3

--- Page 211 ---
respect of smooth movement of vehicles in newspapers and on online
platforms to ensure that no hardship or inconvenience is caused to
the public in the course of traveling within the city. The order
will be issued today to ensure that the decision receives publicity
and that there is ample clarity on the prevailing circumstances.
10. During the course of hearing, it was suggested, and learned
senior counsel and counsel for the parties were ad idem, that it is
high time basic amenities were provided to those engaged in
peaceful and lawful protest. To that end, suitable alternative
sites capable of housing such infrastructure need to be identified
and  designated.  Let  the  Competent  Authority  consider  this
suggestion and take an appropriate decision thereon.
11. Let a compliance report be filed by the Delhi Metro Rail
Corporation, the requisite Railway authorities and Delhi Police
(Traffic) in this regard within four days. 
12. Ordered accordingly.
(NITIN TALREJA)                           (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 229197/2026
1.  Heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsels  assisted  by  the  learned  advocates
appearing along with them.
2. The prayer sought for in the present application is similar and identical to the
prayer that was sought for in IA No.269508/2025 which has been disposed of by
this Court by Order dated 30.10.2025 by granting relief and observing as under:
“6. Upon hearing, we find that Udayasthamana Pooja  was
being performed on Vrishchikam Ekadasi since long. It is to
observe that any ritual which is being performed at any place
or site of worship as part of long-standing tradition, and has
assumed religious significance, ought not be unsettled on the
apprehension  that  there  would  be  potential  public
inconvenience. The faith of the worshippers at large ought
not  to  be  put  aside  on  the  anvil  of  managerial  and
administrative concerns and must be given precedence and
respect as far as possible. The Guruvayur temple has a rich
religious  historical  background  and  a  large  number  of
devotees depose their faith in the deity. The temple has long
run customs, practices and rituals, which if affected, might
run scramble through the sentiments of the devotees/people.
7. It is to be noted that, the performance of the pooja by
Acharyas is conducted for enhancing the divinity of deity. On
special  occasions  such  as  Vrishchikam  Ekadasi,
inconvenience  to  public  cannot  be  a  ground  to
discontinue/alter the rituals/pooja to be performed on the said
day  for  deity.  Thus,  at  this  juncture,  for  the  purposes  of
interim relief, we are not convinced by the reasons stated by
the respondents.
8. In this view of the matter, subject to final outcome of the
appeal,  by  way  of  interim  measure,  we  direct  that
Udayasthamana Pooja shall be continued in the manner as it
was being performed as per the tradition of the temple on
Vrishchikam Ekadasi without any change. In case the Thantri
is  of  the  view  that  Udayasthamana  Pooja  has  also  to  be
performed on 02.11.2025 as stated in the counter affidavit,
he may do so. The Interlocutory Application is accordingly
disposed of.”
3

--- Page 219 ---
3. In the light of the aforesaid order passed and subject to the final outcome of
the  appeal  that  is  pending  by  way  of  interim  relief,  we  direct  that  the
Udayasthamana  Pooja shall  be  continued  in  the  manner  as  it  was  being
performed as per the tradition/custom/practice of the temple on  Vrishchikam
Ekadasi falling on 21.11.2026 without any change.
4.  However,  we  grant  liberty  to  Devaswom  Board  and  also  Tantri  that
Udayasthamana Pooja can also be performed on 22.10.2026 as indicated in the
revised Panchangam.
5. The application stands disposed of accordingly.
Hearing of the appeal is ordered to be expedited.

aggrieved  by  the  impugned  judgment  dated  30.09.2024
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Karnataka  in  RFA
No.392/2023, whereby, the suit was decreed in favour of
the respondent, who is the plaintiff.  Vide the impugned
order,  the  judgment  rendered  by  the  Trial  Court,
dismissing the suit for permanent injunction was set
aside.  Additionally, the Trial Court had granted the
relief  of  possession  in  favour  of  the  appellant-
defendant qua the suit schedule property and directed
the respondent-plaintiff to handover vacant possession
of the same.  The same was reversed by the High Court.
Aggrieved, the appellant is before this Court.

appellant  and  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent at length.

--- Page 229 ---
4. Upon hearing the submissions made at the Bar, it is
agreed that the matter will be disposed of in the
following terms -
(i) The  appellant-defendant  shall  pay  a  sum  of
Rs.25,00,000/-  (Rupees  Twenty  Five  Lakhs)  to  the
respondent-plaintiff by way of Demand Draft, within a
period of four weeks from the date of receipt of a copy
of this order.
(ii) Upon receipt of the said amount, the respondent-
plaintiff shall hand over the vacant possession of the
suit  property  to  the  appellant-defendant,  within  a
period of four months, thereafter.
(iii) In view of the agreed terms, all disputes and
pending proceedings, both civil and criminal in nature,
initiated  by  the  parties  and  their  family  members
against each other, shall stand terminated.  Further,
the parties shall not initiate any further proceedings
either civil or criminal in nature, against each other.
5.  In  view  of  the  aforesaid  settlement  arrived  at
between the parties, the impugned judgment passed by the
High Court stands set aside.
6. Liberty is granted to the parties to approach this
Court, in the event of non-compliance of this order or
any of the terms of aforestated settlement.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).        OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO(S). 12757/2026)
ZONUNMAWII RENTHLEI                                APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
R. LALLUAHSANGI                                    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellant. Despite service, none appears on behalf of the
respondent.
3. Despite the time granted even after the service of notice
for the appearance of the respondent, the same question
continues  even  today.  In  fact,  apart  from  the  earlier
accommodation,  the  matter  was  passed  over  even  today.
Unfortunately, there is no representation on behalf of the
respondent.
4. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits that
though the delay appears to be huge, the High Court has

--- Page 245 ---
2
committed an error in not taking note of the fact the Heirship
Certificate was issued to the respondent vide order dated
22.03.2021 without arraying the appellant as a party and,
therefore, admittedly she was not heard. In such view of the
matter, the delay has to be considered from that perspective.
5. In as much as the order under challenge before the High
Court was passed without notice to the appellant, the question
of delay cannot be considered on extraneous considerations,
what is required to be considered is the date of knowledge of
the  previous  order,  passed  by  the  Civil  Judge,  dated
22.03.2021 wherein the heirship certificate was issued.
6. When  we  consider  the  said  issue  of  knowledge,  the
question of probability does not arise. The Courts have to
take the pleadings as they stand, in the absence of any
contrary material. Even otherwise, we are dealing with the
case where the appellant was not heard and is aggrieved by the
order passed by the High Court.
7. Taking note of the facts and circumstances of the case, we
are inclined to set aside the impugned judgment passed by the
High Court and condone the delay of 1387 days in filing the
regular first appeal before the High Court.
8. Accordingly, the application for condonation of delay

--- Page 246 ---
3
stands allowed and the delay stands condoned.
9.  The High Court is directed to decide the matter on merits,
in accordance with law.
10. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

“6. The petitioner and Respondent No. 1      ...xxx...       between the

a. That the parties have agreed that this settlement forms the
full and final settlement of all past, present and future claims
of  the  Petitioner  against  the  Respondents,  and  no  other
demand will be made by him or on his behalf.

Courts  below  to  the  Petitioner  in  and  around  the  year
2024/2025,  and  the  aforementioned  sum  of  money
comprised of the amount deposited by the Respondent No. 1
in the Court as well as the accrued interest thereupon. 
c. That it has been brought to the fore that the Petitioner had
suffered a 75% damage  to his brain and was bed-ridden
most of the time, and upon release of the deposited amount
to the Petitioner, the same was spent mostly on his medical
expenses and it would not be possible to give a hiatus to the
litigations  between  the  parties  unless  the  matter  was
amicably settled.
d. That accordingly the parties have amicably agreed that the
amount of Rs. 39,86,669/- already received the Petitioner
would be the full and final settlement amount, and that the
Petitioner would not seek or ask for any enhanced amount
more than the said amount of Rs. 39, 86,669/- which had

the amount deposited by them in relation to this case.

against each other or against the family members/ assigns
of each other in respect of the present dispute in future.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No.18357 of 2025)
VAISHNAVI S. UGADEKAR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF GOA & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The dispute pertains to selection for the post
of Coach (Grade-IV) in weightlifting in the State of
Goa. In the course of the selection process, a
dispute arose as to the fairness of the selection
process, upon which the appellant raised a complaint
before  the  Competent  Authority  of  the  State
Government, leading to a direction to re-conduct the
tests.
3. Thereafter, respondent No. 4 preferred a Writ
Petition in which the impugned order has been passed
without impleading or affording any opportunity of
hearing to the appellant.
4. Considering that the appellant and respondent
No. 4 are the only two candidates competing for the
post, we deem it appropriate to direct the High Court
1

--- Page 261 ---
to  decide  the  matter  afresh  after  affording  an
opportunity of hearing to both parties. Consequently,
the  impugned  order  is  set  aside,  and  the  Writ
Petition preferred by respondent No. 4 is restored to
its original number for a decision afresh on merits
upon  hearing  all  parties  to  the  Writ  Petition,
including  the  present  appellant  who  shall  be
impleaded as a party before the High Court.
5. We request the High Court to decide the matter
at the earliest. The interim order passed by this
Court shall remain in operation during the pendency
of the Writ Petition.
6. It is made clear that the High Court shall not
be influenced either by its own previous order or by
this order, and the matter shall be decided afresh on
its own merits.
7. The appeal is disposed of in the above terms.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.
